transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I guess what finally made me come in is my eating has just been... not normal for me lately. It’s kind of all over the place. Some weeks I’ll barely touch dinner, like I’ll make it or sit down with it and then just push it around, and other nights it’s the complete opposite. I’ll be standing in the kitchen after everyone’s gone to bed, eating crackers or sweets, just sort of picking at things and then realizing I’ve been doing it for a while.

It’s embarrassing to say because it sounds small, maybe, but it’s been noticeable enough that I thought, okay, something is off and I should probably talk to someone before it gets worse.
Can you describe what typically happens before and after these nighttime eating episodes? Do you ever try to compensate for them, like by skipping meals, exercising more, or making yourself vomit?

Usually before it happens, it’s just been one of those days where my eating is already off. Like, sometimes I barely eat dinner, or I sit there with the plate and I’m not really interested in it, and then later at night, after everyone’s gone to bed and the house is quiet, I end up in the kitchen. I’ll tell myself I’m just getting a drink or maybe one little thing, and then it turns into crackers or something sweet, just picking at things while I’m standing there.

Afterward I mostly feel kind of embarrassed and annoyed with myself, because it feels like I didn’t even make a real decision to eat. It’s not like a planned meal. It’s more like I suddenly notice, oh, I’ve been standing here eating for a while.

As far as compensating… I don’t really have some set thing I do afterward. The bigger pattern is just that my appetite feels all over the place—some weeks barely touching dinner, and other nights doing that kitchen snacking thing after everyone’s asleep. That’s what made me feel like something is off.
When you find yourself eating at night like that, does it feel like you can't stop or control how much you're eating, or does it feel more like you're just nibbling without really thinking about it?

It feels more like nibbling without really thinking about it, I think. I don’t know if I’d describe it as completely out of control, like I’m panicking or shoveling food in or anything like that. It’s more that I’ll be in the kitchen after everyone’s gone to bed, and I’ll start with crackers or something sweet, and then I sort of lose track of it. Not in a dramatic way, just… I realize I’ve been standing there eating longer than I meant to.

That’s part of why it bothered me enough to come in, because my eating has been so inconsistent. Some weeks I barely touch dinner, and then other nights I’m doing that late-night kitchen thing, and it doesn’t feel like a normal appetite pattern for me.
Do these nighttime eating episodes usually happen after a stressful or emotionally difficult day, or do they seem to happen regardless of how your day went emotionally?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I keep trying to look back and figure out if it’s always after a bad day, and I can’t say there’s a clean pattern like that. What I’ve noticed more is just that my appetite itself has been all over the place.

Like, some weeks I’ll barely touch dinner, even if I made it or I know I should eat, and then other nights I’m suddenly in the kitchen after everyone’s gone to bed, eating crackers or sweets and sort of grazing. It’s not always that I can point to one stressful thing and say, “That’s why I did it.” Sometimes it just seems to happen because I didn’t really eat normally earlier, or because I’m up and the house is quiet, and then I’m picking at things.

So I guess emotionally difficult days might make it easier to happen, maybe, but I don’t know that it only happens then. The main thing that pushed me to come in is just how inconsistent it’s gotten.
Do you usually only find yourself eating like this at night because you're awake, or does it also happen during the day when you're up and about?

It’s mostly at night, from what I’ve noticed. I mean, during the day my eating can still be strange in the sense that sometimes I just don’t really eat much, or I’ll sort of ignore meals, but the standing-in-the-kitchen thing with crackers or something sweet is usually after everyone’s gone to bed.

I think the quiet of the house has something to do with it, or just the fact that I’m still awake and there’s no real structure then. It’s not like I’m out during the day and suddenly doing that same grazing thing in the middle of everything. During the day it’s more that I might not be hungry or I don’t finish food. Then later at night it kind of swings the other way, and I’m picking at stuff without really meaning to.

That’s what finally made me feel like I should come in, because it’s been all over the place—some weeks I barely touch dinner, and then other nights I’m standing there eating crackers and sweets after everyone’s asleep.
Do you often find yourself not feeling hungry during the day, or not having any interest in eating even when you know you should?

Yeah, I do think that happens, at least some of the time. During the day I can kind of go through the motions and not really feel hungry, or I’ll know it’s dinnertime and I should eat something, but I just don’t have much interest in it. It’s not like I’m making a decision to skip meals in some organized way, it’s more like food just doesn’t appeal to me, or I put it off and then suddenly realize I barely ate.

And then that’s part of what’s been so confusing, because it doesn’t stay that way consistently. Some weeks I’m barely touching dinner, and then other nights it flips around and I’m standing in the kitchen after everyone’s gone to bed eating crackers or something sweet. Not a real meal, just picking at things. That back-and-forth is really what finally made me think, okay, this isn’t just a normal appetite thing for me.
When you find yourself eating at night after everyone’s gone to bed, is it usually because you feel physically hungry, or do you sometimes eat even when you’re not really hungry?

It’s kind of both, but I don’t think it’s always true physical hunger. Sometimes I’ll realize, well, I barely ate dinner or I didn’t really eat much earlier, so maybe part of it is my body catching up. But other times I’m not sitting there thinking, “I’m starving.” It’s more like I’m awake, the house is quiet, and then I’m just standing in the kitchen eating crackers or something sweet almost before I’ve really decided to.

That’s what’s been bothering me, I guess—the inconsistency. Some weeks I barely touch dinner, and then other nights after everyone’s gone to bed I’m grazing on stuff like crackers and sweets. It doesn’t feel like a normal meal or a planned snack. It’s more like my eating is just all over the place, and that’s honestly what finally pushed me to come in.

When you find yourself eating in the kitchen at night after everyone’s gone to bed, are you fully awake and aware of what you're doing, or does it feel like you're in a kind of daze or not completely present?

I think I’m awake, mostly. It doesn’t feel like I’m sleepwalking or anything like that. I know I’m in the kitchen, I know I’m opening things and eating them. But it can feel sort of automatic, if that makes sense—like I’m not sitting down and deciding, “I’m going to have a snack now.” It’s more like I’m up, the house is quiet, everyone’s asleep, and then I realize I’m standing there with crackers or something sweet.

So I’m aware, but not very intentional. And that’s part of what’s been bothering me, because it’s not just one clear pattern. Some weeks I’m barely touching dinner, like I’ll just have no interest and leave most of it, and then other nights it’s the opposite where I’m in the kitchen late eating little things after everyone has gone to bed. It’s not like a normal meal. It’s more this grazing thing, and it feels kind of scattered.

That’s really what pushed me to come in, honestly. It just started feeling like my eating was all over the place, and I couldn’t tell if I should be worried or if I was just being dramatic about it.
How often would you say these nighttime eating episodes happen—like, how many nights a week or month do you find yourself eating like this after everyone has gone to bed?

I’m not sure I could give you an exact number, honestly. It’s not every single night, but it’s enough that I started noticing it as a pattern. Some weeks it might happen a few nights, especially if I’ve barely eaten dinner or just picked at it, and then other weeks it’s less obvious.

It’s more that my eating feels really inconsistent. Like, I’ll have days where dinner just doesn’t appeal to me and I leave most of it, and then other nights, after everyone’s gone to bed, I’ll find myself in the kitchen eating crackers or something sweet. Not sitting down for a meal, just kind of grazing. That back-and-forth is really what pushed me to come in, because I couldn’t tell what was going on with me.
Do you often find that you have little to no appetite during the day, even when it's time for meals like lunch or dinner?

Yeah… I mean, that’s part of what I’m trying to explain, I guess. During the day it’s not always that I feel sick or anything, but meals just don’t appeal to me sometimes. Like dinner especially—I’ll sit there with everyone and kind of pick at it, and then realize I barely ate any of it. Some weeks it feels like I’m barely touching dinner at all.

But then it doesn’t stay consistent, which is what’s confusing me. Because other nights, after everyone’s gone to bed, I’ll be standing in the kitchen eating crackers or something sweet, not like a real meal, just sort of grazing. So it’s not simply “I never have an appetite,” but my eating has been all over the place enough that it started worrying me. That’s really what pushed me to come in.
Have you been feeling down, depressed, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy most days, even if just a little bit?

Yeah… I think so. Not every single minute of every day, but I do go through these stretches where everything in the house just feels kind of gray and heavy. Like I’ll be sitting at the kitchen table, and nothing especially terrible has happened that day, nobody said anything awful, there isn’t some big crisis, but I’ll just feel… empty.

It’s hard to explain because from the outside it probably looks like I’m just sitting there, maybe staring off or being quiet, but inside it feels like the air has gotten heavier somehow. Things I normally might enjoy or at least feel interested in don’t really pull me in the same way during those times. I’m there, but I’m not really feeling much connection to anything.

And then I start questioning myself, like, “Why are you feeling this way? Nothing even happened.” But that doesn’t really make it go away. It’s just this flat, gray feeling that settles over me for a while.
Would you say you feel down, depressed, or have little interest in things most days, even if it's just a mild feeling?

Yes… I’d say most days during those stretches, even if it’s not always dramatic. It’s more like this heaviness settles in. The house feels gray, kind of heavy, and I’ll be sitting at the kitchen table just feeling empty, even though nothing terrible happened that day.

That’s the part that bothers me, because I can’t always point to a reason. It’s not like there was a fight or some big bad news. I’m just sitting there, and everything feels flat and kind of far away. So yes, I think there is a depressed feeling there, even if sometimes it’s mild or I try to tell myself it shouldn’t count because I’m still up and moving around.
Have you noticed any unintentional weight loss or a significant change in your weight recently?

I haven’t really tracked the number closely, so I don’t want to say, like, “I lost exactly this much,” because I honestly don’t know. I haven’t been weighing myself regularly.

But what I have noticed is that my eating has been really all over the place, and that’s what finally pushed me to come in. Some weeks I barely touch dinner — I’ll sit down like I’m going to eat with everyone, and then I just kind of move the food around or take a few bites and feel done. And then other nights, it’s the opposite in this weird way, where after everyone’s gone to bed I’ll end up standing in the kitchen eating crackers or something sweet, not really hungry exactly, just… grazing.

So I don’t know if my weight has changed significantly, but the pattern feels off enough that I’ve been worried about it.
Have you found that you don’t take pleasure in activities you normally enjoy, like hobbies, time with family, or things you used to look forward to?

Yes, I have. That’s actually one of the things that makes me feel unlike myself.

There are things I used to look forward to, not even huge things, just normal parts of my life. Like book club — I used to enjoy reading something and having an opinion about it, even if I didn’t love the book. I liked hearing what everyone else thought. Lately it can feel like another appointment I’m supposed to drag myself to, or I’ll put off reading and then feel guilty about it.

Cooking is like that too. I used to like planning a meal or trying something a little different, and now sometimes it just feels like standing in front of the counter doing a list of tasks. Even going to galleries, which used to feel kind of refreshing for me, can feel like too much effort, like I’m just walking through because I’m supposed to enjoy it.

And the rose beds… that one bothers me. I used to really care about them, checking on them, trimming things back, noticing new growth. Now I’ll see they need attention and I just keep putting it off. It starts to feel less like something I love and more like a chore sitting there waiting for me.
Have you found that you’ve lost interest or pleasure in almost all activities, even ones you used to enjoy?

Yes… I think so. I mean, “almost all” sounds so big when you say it that way, and I don’t want to exaggerate, but it really does feel like most things I used to naturally enjoy have turned into things I’m just supposed to do.

Like book club used to be something I looked forward to. I liked choosing the book, reading a little at night, thinking about what I’d say. Now I’ll see the book sitting there and feel this kind of pressure, like it’s homework I’m already behind on. Cooking is another one. I used to get some pleasure from making a meal, even just chopping things or trying a recipe, and now it can feel like this long list of steps I have to get through.

And galleries… those used to give me a little lift, just getting out and looking at things. Lately I’ll think about going and then it feels like too much effort, or I go and I’m sort of there physically but not really enjoying it. Same with the rose beds. I used to care about them so much, and now I look at them needing attention and just keep putting it off. It all starts feeling like chores, even the things that used to feel like mine.
Have you noticed that you’ve been feeling a lack of energy or feeling fatigued most days, even when you haven’t done anything physically taxing?

I’m not sure I’d call it fatigue exactly. I mean, I do have days where I feel kind of slowed down or like it takes me longer to get started, but I haven’t really noticed a clear “I’m exhausted most days” feeling, if that makes sense.

Sometimes I’ll sit there thinking I should get up and do something, and it feels harder than it should, but I don’t know if that’s my body being tired or just… not having much drive for it. I’m sleeping and resting, but I wouldn’t say I’m physically wiped out all the time or anything like that. It’s more that things feel like they take more effort than they used to, but I can’t tell if that counts as fatigue.
Have you found yourself feeling worthless or guilty about things more often than not, even when there isn't a clear reason for it?

Yes… I do. It’s not always some huge thing I’ve done, which is almost what makes it feel worse, because I can tell part of me is overreacting, but I still get stuck in it.

Like, I’ll buy an expensive tube of pigment — something I can technically justify, because I do use it, or I tell myself I’ll use it — and then afterward I’ll sit there thinking, Why did I do that? That was selfish. That was irresponsible. And then it spirals into this whole thing where I feel like I’ve damaged the household somehow, like one purchase means I’ve thrown everything off or made life harder for everyone. Even if no one is saying that to me.

Or if I snap at my spouse, even just a short tone or one irritated comment, I can replay it for hours. I’ll go back over exactly what I said, how my face probably looked, whether I sounded cruel, whether I made the whole house feel tense. And then it stops being “I was a little short with someone” and starts feeling like “I ruin things. I make everything harder. I’m the reason the mood in the house is bad.”

I know, logically, that buying paint or being irritable once shouldn’t mean I’m a terrible person. But emotionally it can really feel that way. I can spend so much time going over it that it’s like I’m trying to punish myself by thinking about it enough.
Have you noticed that your movements or speech have been slowed down, or that you feel restless or fidgety most days?

I don’t know that I notice it as “slowed down,” exactly. If anything, when I’m at my busiest, it goes the other direction — I get sort of wound up in doing things and planning things.

Like, I’ll have a day where I sign up for a committee, then message a bunch of people about a workshop idea, then start three different blog drafts because suddenly they all seem important, and then I’m out there making these huge plans for the garden, like I’m going to reorganize the whole thing. And in the moment it doesn’t feel strange, exactly — it feels productive, like I’m finally getting traction.

But then when I look at it afterward, it’s a lot for one day. It’s not just “I did an errand” or “I made a plan.” It’s like I’m stacking things up, one after another, and I’m very driven to get them all started. So I don’t know about my movements or speech being slowed, but there are definitely times where I’m much more active and restless in that goal-oriented way.
Have you found that you’ve completely lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, like hobbies, time with family, or things you looked forward to?

Yeah… I wouldn’t say completely, like I never enjoy anything at all, but there’s definitely been a loss of interest. Things I used to actually look forward to can feel like another task on a list now.

Book club is a good example. I used to like having the book picked out, making notes, thinking about what I wanted to say, even just seeing everyone and hearing other people’s takes. Lately it’s more like, Oh, I have to finish the chapters, I have to get myself there, I have to talk. And then I put it off, or I don’t read as much, and it starts feeling like an obligation instead of something pleasant.

Cooking too. I used to enjoy planning something nice, especially if I had time to do it properly, but now even that can feel like a chore — chopping, cleaning up, deciding what to make. Same with going to galleries. That used to feel like a treat, like something that would wake me up a little. Now I can think, We should go, I would probably like it once I’m there, but then I don’t actually make the effort.

And the rose beds… I feel bad even saying that, because I do care about them. I used to really enjoy tending them, checking the leaves, deadheading, noticing what was blooming. But lately I’ll see they need attention and I just sort of… avoid it. It becomes one more thing I’m not doing. So no, not a total complete loss, but a lot of the things that used to feel rewarding now feel like chores I keep putting off.
Have you found that you’ve completely lost interest or pleasure in all activities you used to enjoy, including things you looked forward to regularly?

I don’t think I’d say completely lost interest in all of it, no. It’s more like… the things that used to have some pull to them don’t really pull me the same way anymore.

Like book club — I used to look forward to it, not just the people but the whole ritual of reading the book and having something to say. Now I can see it coming up on the calendar and it feels like homework. Cooking is like that too. I used to enjoy making something nice, and now deciding what to make and getting through all the steps just feels like another chore.

Even galleries, which used to feel like a real treat, I’ll think, Oh, that would probably be good for me, and then I just don’t go. And the rose beds… I still care about them, but tending them doesn’t feel peaceful the way it used to. I notice what needs doing and then put it off, and then feel bad that I’m putting it off.

So not completely all pleasure gone, but a lot of things I used to look forward to now feel like chores I keep avoiding.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. Not every single minute of every day, but I do go through these stretches where everything in the house just feels kind of gray and heavy. Like I’ll be sitting at the kitchen table, and nothing especially terrible has happened that day, nobody said anything awful, there isn’t some big crisis, but I’ll just feel… empty.

It’s hard to explain because from the outside it probably looks like I’m just sitting there, maybe staring off or being quiet, but inside it feels like the air has gotten heavier somehow. Things I normally might enjoy or at least feel interested in don’t really pull me in the same way during those times. I’m there, but I’m not really feeling much connection to anything.

And then I start questioning myself, like, “Why are you feeling this way? Nothing even happened.” But that doesn’t really make it go away. It’s just this flat, gray feeling that settles over me for a while.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a depressed mood most days, which would support a diagnosis of major depressive disorder (F43.2x) over eating disorders (F50.8, F50.9).

Yes, I have. That’s actually one of the things that makes me feel unlike myself.

Even going to galleries, which used to feel kind of refreshing for me, can feel like too much effort, like I’m just walking through because I’m supposed to enjoy it.

And the rose beds… that one bothers me. I used to really care about them, checking on them, trimming things back, noticing new growth. Now I’ll see they need attention and I just keep putting it off. It starts to feel less like something I love and more like a chore sitting there waiting for me.

It’s more that things feel like they take more effort than they used to, but I can’t tell if that counts as fatigue.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a feeling of worthlessness or excessive guilt almost every day, which would support a diagnosis of major depressive disorder (F32.9).

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I can spend hours replaying small things, like buying an expensive tube of pigment or snapping at my spouse, and feel like I’ve ruined the whole household because of it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking directly about frequent feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt without a clear reason.

patient.answer:
Yes… I do. It’s not always some huge thing I’ve done, which is almost what makes it feel worse, because I can tell part of me is overreacting, but I still get stuck in it.

Like, I’ll buy an expensive tube of pigment — something I can technically justify, because I do use it, or I tell myself I’ll use it — and then afterward I’ll sit there thinking, Why did I do that? That was selfish. That was irresponsible. And then it spirals into this whole thing where I feel like I’ve damaged the household somehow, like one purchase means I’ve thrown everything off or made life harder for everyone. Even if no one is saying that to me.

Or if I snap at my spouse, even just a short tone or one irritated comment, I can replay it for hours. I’ll go back over exactly what I said, how my face probably looked, whether I sounded cruel, whether I made the whole house feel tense. And then it stops being “I was a little short with someone” and starts feeling like “I ruin things. I make everything harder. I’m the reason the mood in the house is bad.”

I know, logically, that buying paint or being irritable once shouldn’t mean I’m a terrible person. But emotionally it can really feel that way. I can spend so much time going over it that it’s like I’m trying to punish myself by thinking about it enough.

doctor.intent: Assess the presence and severity of psychomotor agitation or retardation, which would support a diagnosis of major depressive disorder.

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: At my busiest I sign up for committees, message people about workshops, start several blog drafts, and make big plans for the garden all in the same day.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I notice it as “slowed down,” exactly. If anything, when I’m at my busiest, it goes the other direction — I get sort of wound up in doing things and planning things.

Like, I’ll have a day where I sign up for a committee, then message a bunch of people about a workshop idea, then start three different blog drafts because suddenly they all seem important, and then I’m out there making these huge plans for the garden, like I’m going to reorganize the whole thing. And in the moment it doesn’t feel strange, exactly — it feels productive, like I’m finally getting traction.

But then when I look at it afterward, it’s a lot for one day. It’s not just “I did an errand” or “I made a plan.” It’s like I’m stacking things up, one after another, and I’m very driven to get them all started. So I don’t know about my movements or speech being slowed, but there are definitely times where I’m much more active and restless in that goal-oriented way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant decrease in interest or pleasure in activities, a key symptom of major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you found that you’ve completely lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, like hobbies, time with family, or things you looked forward to?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: Things I used to look forward to, like book club, cooking, galleries, and tending the rose beds, can just feel like chores I keep putting off.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about losing interest in previously enjoyed activities and things the patient used to look forward to.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I wouldn’t say completely, like I never enjoy anything at all, but there’s definitely been a loss of interest. Things I used to actually look forward to can feel like another task on a list now.

Book club is a good example. I used to like having the book picked out, making notes, thinking about what I wanted to say, even just seeing everyone and hearing other people’s takes. Lately it’s more like, Oh, I have to finish the chapters, I have to get myself there, I have to talk. And then I put it off, or I don’t read as much, and it starts feeling like an obligation instead of something pleasant.

Cooking too. I used to enjoy planning something nice, especially if I had time to do it properly, but now even that can feel like a chore — chopping, cleaning up, deciding what to make. Same with going to galleries. That used to feel like a treat, like something that would wake me up a little. Now I can think, We should go, I would probably like it once I’m there, but then I don’t actually make the effort.

And the rose beds… I feel bad even saying that, because I do care about them. I used to really enjoy tending them, checking the leaves, deadheading, noticing what was blooming. But lately I’ll see they need attention and I just sort of… avoid it. It becomes one more thing I’m not doing. So no, not a total complete loss, but a lot of the things that used to feel rewarding now feel like chores I keep putting off.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant loss of interest or pleasure in all activities, which would support anhedonia as part of a major depressive episode.

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: Things I used to look forward to, like book club, cooking, galleries, and tending the rose beds, can just feel like chores I keep putting off.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly asking about loss of interest or pleasure in previously enjoyed activities.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I’d say completely lost interest in all of it, no. It’s more like… the things that used to have some pull to them don’t really pull me the same way anymore.

Like book club — I used to look forward to it, not just the people but the whole ritual of reading the book and having something to say. Now I can see it coming up on the calendar and it feels like homework. Cooking is like that too. I used to enjoy making something nice, and now deciding what to make and getting through all the steps just feels like another chore.

Even galleries, which used to feel like a real treat, I’ll think, Oh, that would probably be good for me, and then I just don’t go. And the rose beds… I still care about them, but tending them doesn’t feel peaceful the way it used to. I notice what needs doing and then put it off, and then feel bad that I’m putting it off.

So not completely all pleasure gone, but a lot of things I used to look forward to now feel like chores I keep avoiding.
